name: Biceps curl

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Elbow flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric elbow-flexion torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 95°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 32–120° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° and horizontally adducted 20°, not hanging as in a standing curl. Peak torque default: the paper's mean over all participants (65 Nm; men 85 Nm, women 48 Nm). Cross-check: Tsunoda et al. found the peak at 60° of flexion in young men and bodybuilders (90° in women), with the upper arm in a different position; this curve's peak may sit too far into flexion for men.
strengthCurve.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001; cross-check: Tsunoda N, O'Hagan F, Sale DG, MacDougall JD (1993). Elbow flexion strength curves in untrained men and women and male bodybuilders. Eur J Appl Physiol 66:235–239 (peak at 60° of flexion in 18 men, 69.5 Nm, and 11 bodybuilders, 93.3 Nm; at 90° in 15 women, 35.4 Nm)

weightsNote: Elbow flexor weights (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis): the shape over the elbow angle follows each muscle's flexion moment arm relative to the three muscles' mean at that angle, scaled so the weight at 90° equals the muscle's level (weightLevel): its normalized potential moment in elbow flexion (muscle size × peak moment arm) relative to the biceps, from Ramsay et al. 2009 (1 : 0.75 : 0.40). If the load is shared to keep the summed squared activation smallest, activation scales with this potential. Why relative: the effort already rises and falls with the elbow's strength, which itself follows the moment arms, so only a muscle's change against its partners shifts its share. Moment arms read off the paper's model curves (forearm neutral) at 20° steps, to about ±0.1 cm; held flat beyond 130°. With the palm up the biceps' moment arm is a few mm larger, palm down a few mm smaller (their Fig. 6); not included here, the grip variants use Coratella et al.'s factors instead.
weightsSource: Murray WM, Delp SL, Buchanan TS (1995). Variation of muscle moment arms with elbow and forearm position. J Biomech 28(5):513–525 (Fig. 4, model; Fig. 6); Ramsay JW, Hunter BV, Gonzalez RV (2009). Muscle moment arm and normalized moment contributions as reference data for musculoskeletal elbow and wrist joint models. J Biomech 42(4):463–473. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2008.11.035 (Fig. 6: normalized potential moments in elbow flexion, biceps 16.8, brachialis 12.6, brachioradialis 6.7, read off)

muscles.name: Biceps brachii
muscles.note: Also supinates the forearm. Its moment arm grows with flexion, but less steeply than the brachioradialis', so its share of the work is largest with the arm fairly straight.
muscles.source: Weights: shape from Murray et al. 1995 (see weightsNote); level from Ramsay et al. 2009. Grip effect: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Toninelli N, Padovan R, Esposito F, Cè E (2023). Biceps brachii and brachioradialis excitation in biceps curl exercise: different handgrips, different synergy. Sports 11(3):64. doi:10.3390/sports11030064 (10 trained men, each grip at its own 8RM, surface EMG, lifting phase)

muscles.name: Brachialis
muscles.note: Pure elbow flexor, works in every grip. Its moment arm grows with flexion at about the group's pace, so its share stays fairly constant.
muscles.source: Weights: shape from Murray et al. 1995 (see weightsNote); level from Ramsay et al. 2009

muscles.name: Brachioradialis
muscles.note: Its moment arm grows the most with flexion (to about 6 cm, the largest of the elbow flexors), so it does more in mid-to-high flexion. Grip: at the same relative effort it is slightly more active with the palms up than neutral or down (Coratella et al.); other studies, at unmatched loads, found no change (Boland et al.) or more with the palms turned down (Kleiber et al., Marcolin et al.).
muscles.source: Weights: shape from Murray et al. 1995 (see weightsNote); level from Ramsay et al. 2009. Grip effect: Kleiber T, Kunz L, Disselhorst-Klug C (2015). Muscular coordination of biceps brachii and brachioradialis in elbow flexion with respect to hand position. Front Physiol 6:215. doi:10.3389/fphys.2015.00215; Boland MR, Spigelman T, Uhl TL (2008). The function of brachioradialis. J Hand Surg Am 33(10):1853–1859; Marcolin G, Panizzolo FA, Petrone N, Moro T, Grigoletto D, Piccolo D, Paoli A (2018). Differences in electromyographic activity of biceps brachii and brachioradialis while performing three variants of curl. PeerJ 6:e5165. doi:10.7717/peerj.5165; Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Toninelli N, Padovan R, Esposito F, Cè E (2023). Biceps brachii and brachioradialis excitation in biceps curl exercise: different handgrips, different synergy. Sports 11(3):64. doi:10.3390/sports11030064 (10 trained men, each grip at its own 8RM, surface EMG, lifting phase)

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Holds the upper arm still against the load's pull on the shoulder.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Forearm nearly vertical. With free weights the load's line of action passes close to the elbow, so the moment arm (and torque) is small.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Forearm near horizontal. Free-weight moment arm is at its maximum here — the classic sticking point.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: The weight moves back over the elbow. Free-weight torque drops off; cables can keep tension here depending on pulley position.

variants.name: Standing dumbbell curl
variants.notes: Gravity always pulls straight down, so torque ∝ sin(elbow angle): near zero at the bottom and top, maximum at 90°.

variants.name: Standing barbell curl
variants.notes: Per arm the torque curve is identical to dumbbells — equipment alone does not change the curve. Differences are the fixed supinated grip, bilateral loading and wrist position.

variants.name: Hammer curl (neutral grip)
variants.notes: Thumbs up. The torque curve is the dumbbell curl's; only the strength and the muscles' shares can change. Measured: neutral and palms-up grips are about equally strong (within about 5%: Guenzkofer et al., Kohn et al., Mandalidis & O'Brien), and the biceps and brachioradialis work at the same levels in both (Kleiber et al.; Boland et al. with fine-wire EMG found no grip effect on the brachioradialis at all). So the data don't support the hammer curl as a brachioradialis exercise. At the same relative effort (each grip at its own 8RM), Coratella et al. even measured less: biceps −11% and brachioradialis −6% compared with palms up, hence the 0.89 and 0.94 factors.

strengthScale.note: neutral vs palms-up, shoulder at 0°: 95–110% depending on the elbow angle (Guenzkofer et al., Table A1). Mandalidis & O'Brien measured neutral 2–5% weaker than palms up (isokinetic, 30 men, arm raised 90°); Kohn et al. found no significant difference. So the two grips are about equally strong. Two other studies found the neutral grip clearly strongest: O'Connell et al. (standing, 90°) 21% above palms up, and Provins & Salter with a handle; the factor here keeps the matched, controlled measurements above.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric); Kohn S, Smart RR, Jakobi JM (2018). Voluntary activation and twitch potentiation of the elbow flexors across supinated, neutral, and pronated forearm orientations. Physiol Rep 6(1):e13560. doi:10.14814/phy2.13560; Mandalidis DG, O'Brien M (2001). Isokinetic strength of the elbow flexors with the forearm in supination and in the neutral position. Isokinetics and Exercise Science 9:111–117 (Table 2: 30 men); contrasting: O'Connell DG, Cooper KA, Richeson SM, Moeller MB, Stephens JW, Key DJ (2021). The effect of forearm position on elbow flexion strength in nursing, occupational, and physical therapy students. Work 69:403–409. doi:10.3233/WOR-213486 (85 students, standing, elbow at 90°: palm up 23.4, neutral 28.2, palm down 17.3 kg); Provins KA, Salter N (1955). Maximum torque exerted about the elbow joint. J Appl Physiol 7(4):393–398 (12 adults, handle grip: mid-position strongest)

variants.name: Reverse curl (palms down)
variants.notes: Palms down. The biceps' tendon wraps around the radius, so it pulls less effectively and the grip is weaker. Does the brachioradialis take over? At the same relative effort (each grip at its own 8RM, trained men), Coratella et al. measured biceps −16% and brachioradialis −5% compared with palms up, hence the 0.84 and 0.95 factors: the reverse curl is harder, but not a brachioradialis exercise. Kleiber et al. (no load) and Marcolin et al. (EZ bar) found more brachioradialis activity, Boland et al. no change; Coratella et al. is the only one that matched the effort.

strengthScale.note: palms down vs palms up, shoulder at 0°: 83–99% depending on the elbow angle (Guenzkofer et al., Table A1, torque). Kohn et al. measured a bigger drop in force (53%) at 70° of elbow flexion, so this may be optimistic. O'Connell et al. (standing, 90°, students) found palms down 26% weaker than palms up, between these values.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric); Kohn S, Smart RR, Jakobi JM (2018). Voluntary activation and twitch potentiation of the elbow flexors across supinated, neutral, and pronated forearm orientations. Physiol Rep 6(1):e13560. doi:10.14814/phy2.13560; cross-check: O'Connell DG, Cooper KA, Richeson SM, Moeller MB, Stephens JW, Key DJ (2021). The effect of forearm position on elbow flexion strength in nursing, occupational, and physical therapy students. Work 69:403–409. doi:10.3233/WOR-213486 (85 students, standing, elbow at 90°: palm up 23.4, neutral 28.2, palm down 17.3 kg)

variants.name: Preacher curl
variants.notes: Tilting the upper arm 45° forward shifts peak torque to ~45° of elbow flexion: hardest in the stretched position, almost unloaded at the top. The pad removes the shoulder stabilising demand.

strengthScale.note: upper arm 45° forward, which shortens the biceps over the shoulder: elbow-flexion strength drops to about 87% around 90° of elbow flexion. Guenzkofer et al. measured supinated elbow flexion with the shoulder at 0° and 60°; 45° is interpolated between them.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.name: Cable curl (low pulley, in front)
variants.notes: The cable pulls towards the pulley instead of straight down. Move the pulley to see how the torque curve's peak shifts and the bottom of the movement gains tension.

variants.name: Bayesian cable curl (pulley behind)
variants.notes: Facing away from the cable with the arm behind the body. The cable keeps a large moment arm in the stretched (bottom) position, which free weights cannot.

strengthScale.note: arm 25° behind the body. Guenzkofer et al. report only marginal differences between −30° and 0° of shoulder flexion, so no correction.
strengthScale.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.name: Band curl (standing on the band)
variants.notes: An elastic band anchored under the feet. Its tension grows as it stretches, so unlike a dumbbell the resistance keeps rising towards the top of the curl. The load slider is the band's tension at 1.4 m stretched length (about its length at the top); slack below 0.75 m. Bands are linear here; real bands stiffen somewhat as they stretch.
